claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.label: Parenchyma cells are generally rhombic dodecahedra, ideal froths tetrakaidecahedra
claims.statement: A perfectly fluid froth of equal cells is divided into Kelvin’s fourteen-sided tetrakaidecahedra, but in plant parenchyma, given restraint and imperfect fluidity, the cells generally take the rhombic dodecahedral form even under symmetrical conditions.

operationalizations.text: Segment equal-sized plant parenchyma cells in 3D, classify face topology and geometry, and compare frequencies of rhombic dodecahedra and fourteen-faced Kelvin-like cells.

Count faces and face shapes of interior cells in symmetrical, near-equal parenchyma. A mode near twelve rhombic faces would support the dodecahedral claim; a mode near fourteen with hexagonal and square faces would support Kelvin's tetrakaidecahedron instead.

obstacles: Few datasets resolve complete cell faces over large parenchyma volumes.
Cells are rarely equal-sized or perfectly symmetric.
Meristem and embryo cells are a young, growing subset of the symmetrical parenchyma the claim is about.
Surface cells must be excluded, because the twelve-versus-fourteen contrast is about interior cells of a bulk foam.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
roles: Embryo volumes whose interior cells can be segmented for the same face census

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
roles: 3D cell segmentations from which face number and neighbour counts of interior cells can be computed

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Open 3D plant-tissue microscopy for cellular polyhedron reconstruction.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
roles: Public volumetric microscopy that may include plant parenchyma.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.label: Twenty-spined Radiolaria have hexagonal symmetry, not Müller's arrangement
claims.statement: In twenty-spined Radiolaria the spines pass through the facets of a modified hexagonal prism, giving a true hexagonal symmetry of two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two whorls of six intermediate spines; Müller's law of five four-spined circles with no polar spine does not properly apply to any case.

operationalizations.text: Digitize 3D spine directions in twenty-spined specimens and fit the hexagonal 2+6+6+6 arrangement against Müller's five four-spined circles using angular residuals. Taxon-level model support would directly confirm which arrangement applies.

Measure the latitudes and counts of the twenty spines. Hexagonal symmetry predicts two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two alternating whorls of six; Müller's arrangement predicts five four-spine circles and no polar spine. A systematic match to one angular template and not the other decides the claim.

obstacles: Suitable intact microscopic 3D specimens may be sparse.
The assertion that Müller's pattern fits no case requires broad taxonomic coverage.
Acantharia, the main living twenty-spined group, are poorly represented in polycystine image databases and their skeletons are rarely preserved.
Older sources are drawings that may already embody one or the other symmetry scheme.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
roles: Radiolarian skeleton images from which spine positions can be digitized where twenty-spined forms are figured.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Public 3D models may permit direct measurement of radial-spine arrangements.

claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.label: Bone is nearly as strong in tension as in compression
claims.statement: Fresh bone resists tearing almost as well as it resists crushing (tensile strength about 9–12 and crushing strength about 13–16 kg per sq. mm), which makes it an economical structural material that can serve equally as tie or strut.

operationalizations.text: Compile matched tensile and compressive ultimate strengths of fresh bone by species, element and orientation, then test whether their ratio is near one and within the stated ranges.

Compare ultimate tensile strength and compressive strength of fresh cortical bone, in kg per square mm, on matched specimens. The claim is confirmed if tension falls near 9-12, compression near 13-16, and the two are close; a large gap, or values far from those bands, would refute it.

obstacles: Fresh-bone paired tests are scattered.
Strength depends strongly on orientation, hydration, age and strain rate.
Open files emphasize tensile tests of elderly human femoral bone; paired crushing tests of fresh bone across vertebrates are scattered in papers.
Dry, embalmed and demineralized specimens shift both strengths relative to fresh bone.

candidate_datasets.name: BoneMechDamage
roles: Cyclic tensile stress-strain curves and fitted parameters for human femoral cortical bone and individual trabeculae

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
roles: Open research datasets that include biomechanical tests of bone.

candidate_datasets.name: MatWeb
roles: Public materials-property database containing bone mechanical-property records.

claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.label: Heavy heads give tall withers spines; heavy tails give tall lumbar-sacral spines
claims.statement: Animals whose head and neck form a large fraction of body weight have large bending moments over the fore-legs and correspondingly tall spines over the withers, whereas animals with light heads and heavy tails (anteaters, Diplodocus) or that are bipedal (kangaroo, Iguanodon) have their tallest spines over the loins and haunches.

operationalizations.text: Across living and fossil vertebrates, estimate regional mass distribution and measure the position and height of neural spines, then test whether anterior and posterior bending moments predict spine-height maxima after phylogenetic correction.

Across terrestrial vertebrates, relate the craniocaudal position of the tallest neural spines to the fraction of body mass in the head and neck versus the tail. Support would be withers spines where the head is heavy and lumbar or sacral spines where the tail is heavy or the animal is bipedal; a single spinal peak unrelated to that mass distribution would refute the prediction.

obstacles: Soft-tissue mass in fossils is reconstructed indirectly.
Muscle leverage is an alternative explanation for tall spines.
Fossil body-mass fractions are estimated from the skeleton itself, which couples the predictor to the measurement.
Display spines and phylogeny can produce tall withers in light-headed species.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Living and fossil skeletal scans for vertebral measurements.
Skeletal scans of living and fossil vertebrates for neural-spine profiles and relative head, neck and tail size

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
roles: CT of additional skeletons for the same spine-height and mass-distribution comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
roles: Public fossil occurrence and taxonomic context.

claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.label: Attached Foraminifera form plane spirals with whorls flattened on the attached side
claims.statement: Most spiral Foraminifera are plane (discoid) spirals because some force keeps the chambers in a plane, especially in forms that live attached to rock or seaweed, whose whorls are flattened on the attached surface; freely floating forms such as Globigerina tend towards helicoid spirals.

operationalizations.text: Classify spiral Foraminifera by habitat/life mode (epiphytic/epilithic attached benthic, free-living benthic, planktonic) and quantify spire height-to-diameter ratio (planispiral vs trochospiral/helicoid) and umbilical/spiral side flattening across species.

Classify species by attached benthic versus free planktonic habit and quantify planarity, attached-side flattening and helical displacement from shell scans. Strong habitat-associated differences after phylogenetic and size controls support the claim; no association or opposite patterns refute it.

Score planispiral versus trochospiral coiling, ventral flattening, and life habit (attached, free benthic, planktonic) across genera, then test the association with a phylogenetic model. The claim is supported if attached species are disproportionately plane and flattened on the attached face while planktonic species are disproportionately helicoid; abundant attached trochospirals or free planispiral plankton would undermine the stated contrast.

obstacles: Many attached benthic Foraminifera (such as Cibicides and Discorbina) are low-trochospiral with one flattened attachment side rather than strictly planispiral, requiring careful separation of discoid flattening from strict bilateral planispirality.
Ecology is correlated with phylogeny and shell construction.
Many species lack public 3D scans.
Attached versus free habit and the flattened face are not fields in the census databases and must be compiled from monographs.
Coiling mode is phylogenetically conserved, so a habit correlation can be a clade effect.

candidate_datasets.name: World Foraminifera Database
roles: Public taxonomy, distributions and ecological information for Foraminifera.
Taxonomic catalogue of living foraminifera that can be joined to published habit and coiling codes

candidate_datasets.name: bforams@mikrotax
roles: Images and morphological characters for benthic tests, including attached and coiled forms

candidate_datasets.name: Foraminifera.eu Project
roles: Provides lateral, umbilical, and spiral view images of benthic (Rotalia, Cibicides, Discorbis) and planktonic (Globigerina) species for measuring spire height and ventral flattening.

candidate_datasets.name: ForCenS
roles: Global surface-sediment census of planktonic species, the floating end of the contrast

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: 3D shell geometry for measuring flattening, planarity and helicity.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
roles: Marine occurrence and assemblage datasets for ecological classification.

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS)
roles: Provides taxonomic classifications and ecological/functional group annotations (benthic vs planktonic) for extant Foraminifera.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.label: Argali horns share a spiral angle but differ in their shearing (helical) component
claims.statement: Among closely allied wild sheep (Argali) the constant angle of the horn's logarithmic spiral is nearly the same, and the species differ chiefly in the helical shearing component.

operationalizations.text: Fit 3D equiangular helices (cone/helical shear angle plus planar logarithmic spiral angle) to horn scans and museum images of argali subspecies/species (Ovis ammon ammon, O. a. polii, O. a. hodgsoni) and test whether inter-taxon variance lies primarily in the axial shearing/torsion parameter rather than the planar spiral angle.

Decompose 3D horn centerlines from Ovis ammon, O. poli and O. hodgsoni into planar logarithmic angle and out-of-plane helical components. Similar estimated spiral angles but significantly different torsion support the claim; substantial angle differences or similar torsion refute it.

Decompose each argali horn into a logarithmic angle in the generating plane and a helical pitch, then compare Ovis ammon, O. poli, and O. hodgsoni. The claim is supported if the logarithmic angles agree within measurement error while pitch differs; a species difference in the logarithmic angle as large as the difference in pitch would refute the stated partition.

obstacles: 3D scans of all three specific geographic forms of Ovis ammon have modest sample sizes in open 3D archives, though supplemented by extensive museum photography.
Public 3D sample sizes for rare wild sheep may be small.
Taxonomic synonymy and specimen age require curation.
Complete sheaths of all three named argali are scarce in open 3D repositories.
Single photographs confound the in-plane angle with the helical component.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Hosts 3D scans of Ovis ammon and related caprine horns for 3D spiral and helical parameter extraction.
3D wild-sheep horn media for separating curvature and torsion.
Any open 3D Ovis crania from which spiral angle and helical pitch can be separated

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
roles: Digitized museum specimens for taxonomic replication.
Specimen photographs of Asiatic wild sheep for a coarser two-view estimate

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF)
roles: Provides digitized museum horn specimens and photographs of Central Asian Ovis ammon populations (Marco Polo, Tibetan, and Altai argali).

claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.label: A pullet's first eggs are smaller and rounder than its later ones
claims.statement: In the domestic fowl egg size and shape are directly related: a young pullet's first eggs are smaller and more nearly spherical than later ones, and breeds laying relatively smaller eggs lay rounder eggs.

operationalizations.text: Analyze hen-level longitudinal laying records with egg mass and shape index, testing whether first eggs are smaller and rounder than later eggs and whether breeds with smaller relative eggs have rounder shapes. Consistent within-hen trajectories and breed effects support the claim; absent or reversed effects refute it.

Within domestic fowl, compare egg mass and a roundness index between a pullet's first eggs and her later eggs, and among breeds that differ in relative egg size. The claim is confirmed if first eggs are both smaller and rounder, and if breeds laying smaller eggs relative to body size lay rounder ones; either association failing would refute the corresponding half.

obstacles: Public poultry datasets often omit egg shape or exact laying order.
Feed, age, housing and selection line confound breed comparisons.
Cross-species egg tables collapse Gallus to a single average and omit laying sequence.
Breed and age series exist mainly as tables inside poultry papers and would have to be compiled.

candidate_datasets.name: Ag Data Commons
roles: Public agricultural research datasets that may include poultry egg production and quality measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
roles: Open animal-science datasets potentially containing repeated egg measurements.

claims.label: Brachiopod spiral arm direction follows shell shape through spatial constraint
claims.statement: The form and direction of brachiopod spiral arms (brachidia) are determined by their initial curvature and the space and pressures within the shell, so that long outwardly directed spirals should go with transversely elongated shells such as Spirifer, inwardly directed spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with strongly flattened shells.

operationalizations.text: Reconstruct shell interior and brachidium geometry across spire-bearing brachiopods, quantify shell elongation and flattening, and test the predicted association with outward, inward or discoid spiral direction. Phylogenetically controlled models should compare spatial constraint with clade-specific development.

Pair brachidial spiral direction and form with shell outline across spire-bearing brachiopods: outward spirals with transverse shells such as Spirifer, inward spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with flattened shells. The association is supported or refuted by that cross-tabulation; the pressure mechanism remains an interpretation of the association.

obstacles: Internal brachidia are incompletely preserved.
Shell shape and arm direction are strongly confounded with phylogeny.
Spiral direction and shell shape can be conserved together by ancestry rather than by spatial constraint.
Many specimens preserve the shell outline without the brachidium, so the paired sample is smaller than shell collections.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Open micro-CT models can preserve internal brachidia and external shell shape.
CT of brachiopods in which internal spiral brachidia are visible.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
roles: Public fossil taxonomy and occurrences support sampling across brachiopod groups.
Taxonomic and occurrence framework for the spire-bearing groups being compared.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
roles: Illustrated brachiopods, some with spiralia, for pairing shell shape with spiral direction.

claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.label: Forms of cell-aggregates are shaped chiefly by surface tension toward minimal areas
claims.statement: The forms of cells in contact with one another, and ultimately of tissues, are determined especially by surface tension, which shows itself in the production of surfaces of (relatively) minimal area.

operationalizations.text: Reconstruct cell aggregates, estimate interface areas and tensions, and compare observed tissue geometry with constrained minimal-area predictions and models dominated by adhesion, elasticity, or growth.

In segmented cell aggregates, compare wall areas and junction angles with the minimal-area surfaces expected for the observed cell volumes. Agreement with minimal-area geometry would support the geometric half; systematic excess area or a different angle rule would refute it, while an independent tension measurement would be required to credit surface tension rather than another minimizing agency.

obstacles: Minimal area can emerge from several interacting processes.
The claim's tissue-wide scope exceeds available consistently segmented data.
Minimal-area packing is also predicted by adhesion energy and cortical contractility, which these images do not separate from surface tension.
Plant meristems and a few animal epithelia stand in for tissues in general.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
roles: Open multidimensional tissue imaging for segmentation and interface geometry.
Public epithelial and other tissue volumes in which cell-contact surfaces can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
roles: About 100 confocal volumes of early embryos with cell walls stained, for aggregate geometry from the one-cell stage onward

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
roles: Open 3D confocal stacks and expert segmentations of shoot apical meristems for junction angles and cell-face areas

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Public developmental and tissue-imaging datasets across plants and animals.

claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.label: Polar-furrow arrangements follow relative cell sizes, not species identity
claims.statement: Small changes in the relative sizes of the four cells carry the median partition and its polar furrows through all their possible arrangements, which correspond to those observed in various embryos; these arrangements are physical phenomena distributed without relation to zoological classification, not species characters.

operationalizations.text: Across four-cell embryos, model polar-furrow topology from relative blastomere volumes and test whether size predicts arrangement better than species identity.

At the four-cell stage, predict polar-furrow arrangement from relative blastomere volumes and compare that prediction with a model that assigns arrangements by clade. Arrangements tracking size ratios, with little phylogenetic signal once size is controlled, would support the claim; clade-conserved furrows at the same size ratios would refute it.

obstacles: Cross-phyla image protocols and stage definitions differ.
Lineage-specific adhesion and cleavage programs covary with species.
Molluscs, annelids and coelenterates, where many of the classical furrow variants were drawn, are poorly represented in these databases.
Related species often share egg proportions, so size and classification are not fully independent.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Open volumetric embryo time series for cell size and contact topology.

candidate_datasets.name: Echinobase
roles: Sea-urchin cleavage images as a second phylum for the same comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
roles: Public early-development microscopy across several models.

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
roles: Quantitative early-embryo sets in which cell volumes and contact topology can be measured together

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
roles: Frog four-cell images for furrow class and relative blastomere size

claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.label: Specific differences in form are mainly differences of relative magnitude
claims.statement: The essential differences in form between species of the same group are differences of proportion or relative magnitude (Aristotle's 'excess and defect'), and these are the main cause of specific differences.

operationalizations.text: Decompose interspecific shape differences within clades into size/proportion changes versus topological, meristic and novel-structure changes, then estimate the fraction of diagnostic variation explained by relative magnitudes.

Within genera or classes, partition species differences into relative magnitudes (uniform scaling, shear and simple gradients) versus discrete, localized novelties. The claim is supported if most between-species shape distance lies in the proportional part; a large share of discrete character changes would refute 'mainly'.

obstacles: “Essential” and “main cause” lack thresholds.
Species diagnoses and causal differences are not identical.
What counts as the main cause depends on whether landmarks or presence-absence characters are given priority.
Well-sampled clades are a minority of classes and genera.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
roles: Public taxonomic character matrices and images.
Character matrices that record discrete differences alongside continuous proportions

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Broad 3D morphology for geometric morphometrics.
Three-dimensional specimens of related species for geometric morphometric partitions of shape difference

claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.label: Pollen-grain shape depends on whether walls harden before the tetrad separates
claims.statement: Pollen grains and spores formed as tetrahedral tetrads keep the plane facets and sharp angles of the tetrad if their walls solidify before the grains separate, but become spherical if they separate while still soft.

operationalizations.text: Relate mature pollen or spore sphericity and retained tetrad facets to evidence for wall maturation timing relative to separation across taxa and developmental image series.

Compare mature pollen and spore shape with whether the wall rigidified before the tetrad separated. Grains that hardened in the tetrad keeping plane facets and sharp angles, and grains that separated while soft becoming spherical, would support the claim; spherical grains that hardened in permanent tetrads, or angular grains that separated soft, would refute it.

obstacles: Mature shape alone cannot establish wall-hardening time.
Developmental series and mature morphology are rarely linked for the same taxa.
PalDat records shape and whether grains are united, not the developmental timing of wall hardening relative to separation.
Apertures, harmomegathy and drying also produce facets, and fern and red-algal spores are outside this pollen database.

candidate_datasets.name: PalDat
roles: Public pollen morphology database for scoring mature shape, facets, and tetrad-derived features.
Public pollen micrographs and shape descriptors, including pollen-unit type, for scoring spherical versus faceted grains and tetrad retention

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Open developmental microscopy for wall formation and tetrad separation timing.
